Issue #472: the paired secret half of the matrix. A legacy Supabase service_role JWT carries `"role":"service_role"`, not `"role":"anon"`, so the narrow carve-out does not apply and it is still detected at high confidence.

Issue #472: a `"role":"anon"` claim alone does not exempt a token; the carve-out requires `"iss":"supabase"` together with `"role":"anon"`, so a non-Supabase issuer claiming the anon role is still detected.

Issue #472: the structural matcher bounds only the payload's minimum tail length, not its total length modulo 4. This 9-byte payload segment leaves a 1-sextet base64url remainder, which unpadded base64 can never legitimately produce, so the claim text cannot be decoded and the carve-out does not apply; the token is still detected.

HTTP Basic authorization is excluded from bearer-token specifically: the grammar requires the literal 'bearer' keyword, so a Basic-scheme header never reaches its scheme check. The value is not left unguarded, though — generic-token's broader authorization_credential rule still claims it, the same scheme-agnostic pattern authorization-positive-basic already documents for a bare (non-bearer-token-adjacent) Basic header. This is the Basic-versus-Bearer scheme separation: bearer-token owns only the 'bearer' literal, and a sibling contextual detector covers the rest.
An Authorization header whose Bearer scheme has no following whitespace or value at all is excluded: the required separator never appears, so there is no credential run to measure.

Only a space or a tab separates the Bearer keyword from its credential; a newline is deliberately excluded from that separator charset, so a scheme keyword immediately followed by a line break never reaches a value.
The scheme keyword is matched case-insensitively and a tab is accepted as the separator, not only a space.

Uppercase 'AUTHORIZATION'/'BEARER' keywords and extra whitespace around the header colon and before the credential are all accepted; the case and whitespace policy is flexible on both sides of the scheme.

A secret containing RFC 4648-excluded digits ('0', '1') mid-value truncates the base32 run at the first invalid byte; since the remainder is not all padding, the value is rejected outright rather than matched up to the truncation point.
Padding ('=') appearing before the end of the value, followed by more base32-alphabet characters, is rejected: padding must only ever be a suffix.

Accepted tradeoff: only the first secret= occurrence is ever inspected; when it is below the minimum length the URI is not detected even though a second, syntactically valid secret follows in the same query string. The detector deliberately does not fall back to later duplicate parameters.

Accepted tradeoff: the detector never percent-decodes the query string, so a secret value that percent-encodes its own '=' padding (%3D) is not recognized as base32 and produces no finding, even though the decoded value would be a valid secret.

Accepted tradeoff: the parser matches the literal ASCII bytes "secret=" only; a percent-encoded key byte (%73 for 's') never matches, so the parameter is invisible to the detector even though a URI-aware consumer would decode it identically to "secret=".

Accepted tradeoff: a label containing a literal, un-percent-encoded space (invalid per RFC 3986 but occasionally emitted by non-conforming generators) ends the label scan without the query-string '?' immediately following it, so the whole URI produces no finding even though a genuine secret follows later in the same line.

Accepted tradeoff: a sentence-ending period is not a recognized query terminator, so it is absorbed into the candidate secret value and fails base32 validation, silently suppressing an otherwise-valid secret embedded in prose.

Accepted tradeoff: the otpauth:// scheme is matched as a literal lowercase byte sequence, documented in the detector's module comment as matching real-world generator output; an uppercase-scheme URI, while non-conformant, produces no finding.
An empty secret= value (zero-length) is a near-miss of the true grammar and produces no finding.
A well-formed otpauth:// URI with an unrecognized type segment ('push', neither totp nor hotp) is not matched by either supported prefix.

The body alphabet is [A-Za-z0-9], the same wide alnum class every other infra-provider exact-length shape in this crate uses; an x-filled documentation-style placeholder is built entirely from valid alphabet characters, so it is indistinguishable from a genuine key and is classified, not excluded -- the literal prefix is its own marker, unlike the legacy bare-hex shape.
A body one byte short of the documented 34-byte length is rejected rather than truncated.
A body one byte longer than the documented length is rejected rather than matched up to the documented length.
The documented prefix is the literal lowercase ddapp_; a case-mangled twin is rejected rather than matched.
A ddapp_-prefixed run directly glued to a wider identifier on either side is rejected rather than matched as a substring.

Datadog's own Agent app-key validator, the CloudFormation and ARM templates, and AWS's independent documentation all require a strict [A-Za-z0-9] body; only the Agent's own log-scrubbing replacer is lenient enough to admit an underscore. Worst-case offset map: 2,048 alternating kept/removed code points (U+00AD) make two thirds of the line removed bytes and one seam per kept character, then a provider token split by U+200C follows. Bounds normalization and range translation through the adversarial runtime caps rather than a normalization threshold, which would itself be a bypass; the range is translated across every preceding seam.
